performers: Skidmore College Orchestra, per the Free Music Archive and Internet Archive; not named on the Commons page
question: How does an orchestra make something heavy move closer, pass, and recede?
intro: A Polish ox-cart creaks past: the cart arrives from a distance, passes at full volume and rumbles away. Follow the level as well as the tune. Instruments named here follow Ravel’s orchestration, the probable but undocumented version.

sections.label: The tune at full strength
sections.mNote: opening tune returns, now at the climax

cues.title: A tuba tune from afar
cues.text: A tuba melody, written high in its range, rises out of near silence over trudging strings: the cart approaches from far off. That is the reading of Rimsky-Korsakov and Ravel; Mussorgsky’s piano original starts fortissimo and only then recedes.
cues.evidence: Tuba solo and quiet start: Philharmonia guide and Wayzata Symphony Orchestra note (tuba written high; often played on euphonium); original fortissimo start: Wikipedia’s Pictures at an Exhibition article (Cattle). Relative level −25.0 dB at 0:00; brightness stays between 538 and 600 Hz to 0:40, a dark colour.

cues.title: Poland on Mussorgsky’s mind
cues.text: The Imperial Theatres rejected the first Boris Godunov in 1871. For the 1872 revision Mussorgsky added Marina and the Polish scenes, so Poland, where Hartmann drew in 1868, was already part of his music.
cues.evidence: Site influence edge pushkin-boris-godunov--mussorgsky-boris-1868 (content/influence/romantic.json) for the 10 February 1871 rejection and 1872 revision; the site’s Mussorgsky biography for the added Marina and Polish scenes; Michael Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note for Hartmann at Sandomierz in 1868. The note sits in the quiet opening (−22 dB).

cues.title: The colour brightens
cues.text: At about 0:50 the strongest change in the first minute arrives: the level climbs from −21.8 dB to −13.4 dB by 1:00 and the sound turns brighter, with the dark opening colour replaced by upper instruments.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 0:50 (novelty 0.90) and 0:54; brightness 562 Hz (0:40), 842 (0:45), 1,027 (0:50), 1,427 (0:55); relative level −21.8 dB (0:45) to −13.4 dB (1:00). The report does not identify instruments.

cues.title: Stasov’s ox-cart, and a secret
cues.text: Stasov described “a Polish cart on enormous wheels, drawn by oxen”. Mussorgsky told him the wagon “is not inscribed on the music; that is purely between us”. Hartmann had spent a month at Sandomierz, in Poland, in 1868.
cues.evidence: Stasov’s programme and Mussorgsky’s remark to Stasov, with Hartmann’s month at Sandomierz in 1868: Michael Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note (https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition); also Wikipedia, movement 4. The note sits where the level is rising to the climax (−16.0 dB at 1:10 to −8.1 at 1:20).

cues.title: The peak and the sudden fall
cues.text: The loudest window is 1:30, at −5.6 dB. At 1:40 the level drops by about eight decibels while detected attacks reach their highest rate, above six a second; the cart has passed and only its rattle is left.
cues.evidence: Relative level −5.6 dB (1:30), −7.6 (1:35), −16.0 (1:40); onsets per second 5.4 (1:30), 6.4 (1:40), 6.6 (1:45); boundary at 1:42 (novelty 0.78). A snare drum at the climax is from the Philharmonia guide; the report does not identify it, so the cause of the attack rate is not claimed.

cues.title: Harp and plucked bass
cues.text: In the last half-minute the colour is dark again, about 480 to 590 Hz, and the level sinks from −21 dB to −34 dB. In Ravel’s version a low harp and plucked double bass close the movement as the animals stomp away.
cues.evidence: Low harp and plucked double bass: Philharmonia guide. Brightness 476 Hz (1:50), 516–585 Hz (2:00–2:10); relative level −21.5 dB (1:55), −28.5 (2:00), −34.0 dB (2:15). The report does not identify instruments.

transitions.title: The dark tune gives way to bright strings
transitions.how: The opening tune sinks away and the music brightens as it grows louder: the low, dark colour of the tuba and low strings is replaced by upper instruments, and the bass moves to F♯. This is the middle of the ternary form. The cart is nearer, so Mussorgsky raises both volume and register together, with the walking pulse unchanged beneath.
transitions.evidence: Boundaries at 0:50 (novelty 0.90) and 0:54; brightness 562 Hz (0:40) to 1,427 Hz (0:55); relative level −21.8 dB (0:45) to −13.4 dB (1:00); bass pitch class F♯ at 0:50–0:55. Ternary form: Wikipedia’s article; key labels are confirmation only.

transitions.title: The tune returns with everything
transitions.how: After a dip at 1:10 the level climbs steadily, from −16.0 dB to −5.6 dB at 1:30, and the opening melody comes back in a much heavier scoring. The same tune that began almost inaudibly is now the loudest thing in the movement. The join is a retransition by crescendo: a long, steady build in volume prepares the return of the first material.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 1:16 (novelty 0.70); relative level −16.0 dB (1:10), −11.6 (1:15), −8.1 (1:20), −7.1 (1:25), −5.6 (1:30, the loudest window). The return of the first tune follows the ternary form (Wikipedia); the report cannot confirm the melody itself.

transitions.title: The volume drops and the cart recedes
transitions.how: The climax stops short: the level falls about eight decibels at 1:40 and keeps sinking to −34 dB by 2:15. The colour darkens again to its opening brightness, and low harp and plucked bass take over as the cart recedes. Instead of a cadence, Mussorgsky ends with a long diminuendo, the sound of something heavy going out of earshot.
transitions.evidence: Boundaries at 1:42 (novelty 0.78) and 1:50 (0.75); relative level −7.6 dB (1:35), −16.0 (1:40), −20.3 (1:50), −28.5 (2:00), −34.0 (2:15); brightness 1,334 Hz (1:40) to 476 Hz (1:50). Low harp and plucked bass: Philharmonia guide.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Skidmore College Orchestra (orchestra, as stated by the Free Music Archive; conductor unknown)
fields.note: The Commons page names no performer (“see Musopen for performance author information”). The Free Music Archive album of 15 tracks by the Skidmore College Orchestra lists a track of the same title and length (2:20; this file is 2:19), and the Internet Archive item for the first Promenade credits the same orchestra. The identification of this file with that track rests on title and length; the Musopen performer page was not opened. Conductor: unknown.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: No session date is documented. The Internet Archive item says “date unknown, 2008 at the latest”; the Free Music Archive lists the album as released 6 April 2009; this file was uploaded to Commons on 2008-01-21. None of these is a recording date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No venue is documented. The Free Music Archive biography describes the orchestra as a semi-professional ensemble of Skidmore students and regional professionals; this is not a recording location.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The original release is not identified; Musopen and the Free Music Archive are distribution channels.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Mussorgsky’s piano suite (he died in 1881) is public domain; Commons marks the music PD-old-100. An orchestration is a separate work with its own term and is not cleared here.
fields.note: The Commons notice covers Mussorgsky’s music only. If the version is Ravel’s, his orchestration is not assessed in this dossier.

fields.value: Rule 1 — recording release: PD-author public-domain dedication by Musopen, with Wikimedia VRTS permission ticket 2008012110017088.
fields.note: The file description applies PD-author|Musopen to the recording separately from PD-old-100 for the music, and cites the VRTS ticket; the page is in “Items with VRTS permission confirmed”. Musopen’s reproduced policy says the music is public domain with no restrictions; its requests not to sell the recordings and to credit Musopen are courtesy requests, not a non-commercial licence. The Internet Archive copy of the first Promenade is marked CC0 1.0. Session date is not needed for this route.

composer.epithet: He made Russian speech, public crowds and the noises of ordinary life determine the shape of opera.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition informally with Mily Balakirev; no conservatory education
Guards officer until 1858; civil servant, including work in the Forestry Department
Balakirev, Borodin, Cui and Rimsky-Korsakov; the critic Vladimir Stasov
Operas, dramatic songs and piano music; many works unfinished or published in other composers’ revisions
composer.background:
Mussorgsky grew up on his family’s estate at Karevo, where his mother taught him the piano and his nurse supplied stories that he later associated with his earliest improvisations. The household belonged to the landowning class. The peasant voices he eventually put into songs and operas came from another social world. Sent to Saint Petersburg for schooling, he studied piano with Anton Gerke and entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852. In 1856 he joined the Preobrazhensky Regiment. His first published piano piece, a polka, belonged to the drawing room.

Meeting Dargomyzhsky and then Balakirev redirected that education. Balakirev taught through playing, criticism and the examination of scores. Mussorgsky left the army in 1858, but composing did not provide a living. The emancipation of the serfs in 1861 disrupted the estate income on which his family depended, and he eventually took civil-service posts. The group later called the Five brought together different professions and musical methods: Borodin was a chemist, Cui a military engineer, Rimsky-Korsakov a naval officer. Their shared opposition to imported academic authority concealed substantial musical disagreements.
